A ring of cork fits into this, in which is placed a glass or stoneware stopper. The principle of stopping or closing the orifices of bottles jor other vessels with cork is well understood. Nevertheless, the present method of its application is open to many objec- tions, the consideration of which will serve to illus- trate the superior advantage that the new invention and application of hollow corks present; and as a superior effect is produced, and no new material used, their introduction is not calculated to excite any opposition on the part of those who are in favour of the present or solid corks. The application of hollow corks in reality improves ?? the principle of solid corks, and it is hoped that their superiority will remove the disadvantages which have hitherto ex- isted. The Royal Patent Decorative Glass Works of Southwark Bridge-road show some fine specimens of their new vitrified lace-pattern glass. The process and the effects produced are entirelynovel. Perfect representations of net or muslin curtains, with embroidered borders (correct in every detail), and every description of lace pattern, may be produced by this very ingenious process. The material used for the matt or groundwork is different from that usually employed; it is more even in surface, and will retain its purity of colour without being affected by exposure to the atmosphere, and it has a semi- transparent appearance, not found in any work of a similar character. For internal embellishments it appears to possess decided advantages over other descriptions of white ornamented glass. It has the same appearance from both sides, does not require the aid of a light behind to show the design, and the ornament stands out in strong relief when viewed by artificial light. On Monday, thie 4th inst., the total nmmber of visitors was 62,631, and tho total receipts, 3,028 18s. Yesterday the number of visitors was 58,634, and the receipts 2,835 9s., including 5 10s. for season tickets. This falling-off is very slight, considering 1he enormous numbers who have had an opportunity of visiting the building since its inauguration. ''iie diminution is certainly rather desirable than otherwise, when. it is considered how the denser concourses of a few wecks back, reaching sometimes to between seventy and eighty thousand, precluded a satisfactory examination of the uost interesting objects. The weather yesterday was delightful, and thousands of all classes took advantago of the excursion trains which were started early in the morning from all parts of the country, to accommodate visitors to the Crystal Palace. No fewer than between 18,000 and 19,000 poured in nt the doors during the first hour after they had been opened, and botween eleven and twelve o'clock the crowds admitted had risen to 37,312. Between twelve and one, 9,516 more entered ; between one and two, 5,276; between two and three, 3,080 - between three and four, 1,990 ; between four and five, 1,100; making thte total up to five o'clock, 58,274. We mentioned yesterday that fresh importations of arti- cles for exhibition had arrived on Saturday from the United States. To-day they were in the course of being unpacked. We are informed that they consist of eight or nine more carriages, some five-and-twenty additional cases of agricul- tural implements, such as ploughs, hoes, harrows, rakes, and spades, besides several specimens of cotton-gins which are used in the States for extractiig the seed from the cotton plant. We understand that several of the American light 4 ploughs now exhibited are rapidly getting into great favourI ir, this country. The following is a copy of the letter addressed by the Mlarquis of Normauby to Earl Grauville, in re- ply to the request of his lordship, on behalf of the visitors to Paris, to express to the President of the Republic and the Prefect of the Seine the grateful acknowledgments of the kind and cordial reception which they had met at the hands of all classes in Paris " Paris, August 7. My dear Granville-Pray assure the gentlemen who have signed the letter which you have committed to my charge that I will take the earliest opportunity to communicate the sentiments expressed ir. that paper to the President of the Itepublic and the Prefect of the Seine. " It is my intention to write officially to the Minister for Foreign Affairs on the subject, and also to repeat verbally, beth to the President and to the Prefect of the Seine these expressions of gratitude on the part of the commissioners, jurors, and others connected with the Exhibition. " I em convinced that the Prince, and all the members of his Government, will receive with much satisfaction the assurances that their cordial hospitality has been duly ap- preciated by those to whom it was freely offered, and it is a matter of gratification to me, as the representative of my Sovereign, to be the medium of naling known to the Government to which I am accredited such a declaration on the part of my countrymen. " Having, during the last five years of uninterrupted re- sidence in ithis country, laboured incessantly, under varied circumstances, to promnote a kindly feeling between these two great neighboring people, I receive from you with peculiar pleasure this testinsony of the first beneficial result of the Great Exhibition, in itself so wsell calculated to pro- mote the development of mutual goodwill amongst nations. " The city of Paris on this occasion has displayed no idle or unmeaning hospitality, if frem a survey of its municipal constitution we can gather a full impression of the necessity which exists for reforming that of London, and if from the examination of its magnificent public ?? and institu- norms, founded and liberally supported by Government for the free use of an intelligent people, we can borrow ideas to be realised hereafter, whereby our industrial energies may be directed by the rules of good taste, and a more artistic spirit be harmoniously combined withl the strong utilita- rian tendencies of our manufactures." These very curious and uncommon specimens of taxidermy in fuln and taxidermy in earnest, form undoubtedly -in a small way-one of the most remarkable features of the Exhibition. Thle expression managed to be por- trayed on the faces of the aninmals is semi-human, and yet there is nothing in the slightest degree re- volting or forbidding in the representation. Mon- keys and apes, whose faces resemble in some degree those of men, wye are accustomed to consider as hideously ugly crea. tures, and, indeed, as something degrading to contemplate. Not so the " Comical Creatures from Wurtemburg." The fox, although in look infinitely more sage and more sly thea many of his hunian admirers, is a fox still. The rabbit, too, although his honest hairy face may be a thought less stupid than some whiel stare into it, is also a rabbit still. The animals borrow exaggerated expression, without losing their brute looks; and the r1tioalae of the irresistible risibility which they excite, is the wondrous union of brute face with human expression. InI a previous article upon the Exhibition we alluded to the tendency of the German mind to construct legends of which the loner asnimals were the personages and d'assntis pcrsoltte. Thle qualities of the population of a quiet High.Dutch. village were transferred to hares, weasels, bears, rabbits, foxes, and wolves-with, perhaps, here and there a supernatural old griffiu or dragon; arud the little scandals and incidents of botiseliold life were made over from the chimney-corner and the garden to the forest and the field. Of the many German stories of this class, that of " Leynard the Fox" is the oldest aiid the most famous. Carlyle says, " Among, the people it was long a house-book and universal best companion it lias been lectured on in universities-quoted in impe- rial council halls-it lay on the toilets of princes- and was thumbed to pieces ois the bench of the artLizan. We hear of grave men ranking it next to their Bible." With this rather extravagant degree of admiration we certainly do not coincide. " Reynard the Fox " is a tolerably good piece of well-intentioned whimsicality ; but " Jack the Giant Killer," or " Puss in Boots," is worth a dozen of it. Goethe, however, tolk the story as the subject of a great poem-a fact Wihich, to some extent, we fear, proves that Goethe, in vulgar phrase, must have been very " hard lip " for subjects; amid Kaultachi, the weell-hnown German painter, adorned this poem with a series of thoroughly characteristic pictures, from wihic Herrmannii PlaqUet, the constrictor of the " Comical Creatures from Wtirtemburg," has copied no less titan six of his figures. The other groups of aanimals are what we may call fancy sketches in fur, and are just as oddly hiuman as the copies from KRaulbacli. The stall in which these odd preparations are placed is one of the issost crowded points of the Exhibition, and iithiing can be more genuine thaou the admiration, or more hearty than the laughter, with wvhichi thie civilleed anin.als are greeted. The notion of preserving their forms and expres- sions by means of the unfailing daguerreotype-of multiply- ing the impressions by the help of careful and minuto sood- en3gravings-of expounding and setting forth the legend of " Reyuiard the Fox" by a pleasantly executed translation-of giving a coherence and a literary consistency to the other groups by means of uinpretendilmg little stories invented for thie nonce-the notion, in fine, of embodying all these reminiscences of the Exhibition, and of German fancy and quainit imvention, in a pretty little folio- was an exceedingly happy one, and one which, we doubt not, will be eminently successful. Mr. Bogue, of Fleet-street, has ushered into the world this literary me- mento of the " Comical Creatures from Wurtemburg." The tales other than that of Reynard aspire to little literary nmerit, but they ?? together the subjects of the plates aid give to each a significance and a point which will be readily associated with the piquant expressions of the ani- mals. The drawings are careful and clever, and convey a very correct representation of the original creatures, with all, or nearly all, their subtlety of expression and aspect. The capitsl fatuity of the rabbits and hares, the delight- ful scoundrelism of the fox, the culning shrewdness of the martens and weasels, the hoyden visages of the kittens, and the cool, slippery demeanour of the frogs, are all capitally given. The book is a clever and a pleasant memento of the Exhibition. It may lie on the drawing-roomn table, or be thumbed in the nursery; and in the latter case we have little doubt that minany an urchin still in petticoats will in future years associate his most vivid recollection of the Great Exhi- bitioim of 1851 with Mr-. THE ORIGIN AND HISTORY OF THE GREAT EXHIBITION. lOn Thursday, the great event took place which has for the last sixteen months occupiedin a greater or a lesser degree the attention of the people, not only of this country, but of the civilized world. In the midst of royalty and rank, and all that is great and illustrious in the land, the opening of the Exhibition took place. People of all realms and of all climes will, during the coming months, view with wonder and delight, and with profit and advantage, the rich treasures from the bowels of the earth, the mighty deep, and the realms of animal and vegetable creation, together with the display of mechanical invention, and the productions of industry and art which, collected from the four quarters of the globe, will be there spread out before them. "In other countries and other climes," said the great statesman whose loss the nation yet deplores, "splendid spectacles have been provided for the gratification of the people. There still remain the ruins of ancient edifices, almost uninjured by time, where, for the gratification of the people, showy and costly spectacles were provided. On a Roman holiday hecatombs of wild beasts were slain, and sanguinary conflicts took place of man against man. We propose, however, to gratify the people by other agencies mote in harmony with our civilisation and Christianity—to teach them gratitude to the Almighty Creator by exhibiting the wonderful contrivances of nature for the happiness of man, and to draw closer the bonds of amity and general intercourse, by the honest rivalry of industry and skill." The great success of the last French Exposition caused several representations to be made to members of the Cabin( t of this country, of the benefit which a similar exhibition would be likely to confer on the industry of the United Kingdom, and efbrts were made to obtain the assistance of the G ivernment, but with no apparent results, and no hapes were held out that the Government would be induced to undertake any pecuniary liabilities in the promotion of such an exhibi ion. Even so late as the year 1848, a proposal to establish a self-sudporting exhitoi , ion of Btilish industry, to be controlled by a royal commission, was submitted to his Royal Highness Ptince Albert, and by him laid before the Government, which still hesitated to take up the subject; and it became, therefore, evident to those parties who were most desirous of wimessing the establishment of a national exhibition, that if such an event should ever take place, it would have to be carried out independently of any assistance of that character. The Society of Arts, however, appear steadily to have kept the idea in sight. To assist in carrying out its intention of holding a National Exhibition in the year 1851, the council of the society caused a report on the French Exposition, held in 1849, to be made for them by Mr. D. Wyatt; a petition was also presented by the council to the House of Commons, praying that the society might have the use of some public building for the Exhibition of 1851. At the close of the session of 1849, Prince Albert, who, as president of the Society of Arts, had fully concurred in all the steps taken upon this subject by the society, took the matter more immediately under his own personal superintendence. The enlarged and liberal views which his Royal Highness took upon the subject could not, however, be confined within the compara ively small area of an Exhibition of British Industry. In framing the general outlines of the undertaking, his Royal Highness, at a meeting of several members of the Society of Arts, held at Buckingham Palace on the 30th of June, proposed that the Exhibition should be divided into four sections—the first being raw materials and produce, illustrative of the natural productions on which human industry is employed. The second, machinery for.agriculturing, manufacturing, engineering, and other purposes, and mechanical inventions—idustrative of the agents which human ingenuity brings to bear upon the products of nature. The third, manutactures—illustrative of the result produced by the operation of human industry upon natural produce. And the fon th, sculpture, models, and the plastic arts generally—illustrative of the tastes and skill displayed in such applications. At this meeting also, His Royal Highness pointed out the vacant ground in Hydepark, on the south side, parallel with and between the Kensington-drive and the ride commonly called Rotten-row, as affording advantages whtch few other places might be found to possess, and for which site application could be made to the Crown. It was also decided that a Royal Commission should be issued, of which his Royal Highness Prince Albert should be the head. At this stage of the proceedings it was considered advisable, by the Council of the Society of Arts, to enter at once into pecUniary arrangements calculated to insure the carrying out of the proposed plan. After considerable negociation with several builders and contractors, an agreement was entered into between the Socie, y of Arts and Messrs. Munday, by which the latter undertook to deposit £20,000 as a prize fund, to erect a suitable building, to find offices, to advance the money requisite for all preliminary expenses, and to tade the whole risk of loss on certain conditions. It was proposed thA the receipts arising from the Exhibition should be dealt with as follows :—The £20,000 prize fund, the cost of the building, and the five per cent. on all advances, were to be repa d in the first instance ; the residue was then to be devided into three equal parts; one part was to be paid at onceto the Society of Arts as a fund for future exhibitions: out of the other two parts, all other incidental costs, such as those of general management, preliminary expenses, &c., were to be paid ; and the residue, if any, was to be the remuneration of the contractors for their outlay, trouble, and risk. Subsequently the contractors agreed that instead of this division they would be content to receive such part of the surplus, if any, as, after payment of all expenses, might be awarded to them by arbitration. This, however, was subsequently put aside, and £23,000, with the interest which had accrued, was paid to them as compensation. BOBBIN-NET MACHINERY. -Nottingham, long celebrated for her machine-made lace, has, on this occasion, furnished indubitable proofs that her manufacturers and artisans have been progressing in the same ratio as those in most other branches of industry, during the last half- century. Fifty years ago, lace made by mashinery was mostly from the point-net and warp-machines (both modifications of the original stocking-frame); since that period, there have been incredible sums of money ex- pended, many valuable lives sacrificed by intense study, hundreds of patents taken out, and nearly as many differ- ently-constructed machines built for the production of plain and ornamental lace of every description. It has been matter of astonishment to see how quickly one inventor has succeeded another, and by simplifying or modifying his machines rendered useless those of his predecessor. It may be stated, that in none of the textile fabrics have there been so many combinations of ma- chinery used to effect the purpose as in the making of lace, commencing with the stocking-frame, to which was added a Tickler machine, then the point-net machine, warp machine, Mechlin plait machine, and many others. All of these (except the warp machine,) disappeared for the purpose of making lace when the bobbin-net machine was introduced, and its capabilities for making both plain and ornamnental lace became developed. The bobbin-net ma- chine is so called from the thread that makes the lace being partly supplied from bobbins, and partly from a warp, the bobbins being made to pass from front to back, and back to front, while a lateral motion is imparted to the warp threads, thus causing one series of threads to warp round the other. We to-day continue our descriptions of the articles exhibited in the class devoted to Furniture Decorations, &c., selecting for our present notice the various specimens of oil-cloths exhibited; and we also give some additional information with respect to the beautiful specimens of Statuary Porcelain exhibited, and the process of their manufacture. FURNITURE DECORATIONS.-No. VII. * FLOOR CLOTHS. The floor cloths exhibited are more than creditable to the producers, and are well calculated to convey a most favourable impression of the taste and skill displayed in this branch of manufacture, and which is one of considerable importance in the metropolis. We believe that a century has scarcely elapsed since the first patent was taken out for making floor cloths by block printing, a process identical with that used for the printing of cotton goods and the manufacture of paper-hangings. This patent was obtained by Mr. Smith, the founder of the firm of Smith and Baber, the extensive manufacturers at Knightsbridge, and the process has entirely superseded the old method of producing floor cloths by plates and stencilling. Floorcloths being intended generally for situations where carpets would not be appropriate--where marble or stone floors, cane and India matting, or parquetrie, might be expected to be met with--the most appropriate class of designs are those of a simple and geometric character. The quality of a floor cloth depends even more upon the purity of the paint used than upon the quality of the canvas painted upon. Unadulterated white lead will produce a cloth that will endure almost as long as the stone of which it may possibly form the cover; and the firmness or stiffness of a floor cloth gives no idea of its quality, as a coating of strong size on the canvas previously to commencing to paint it will produce all that may be wished in this respect, and much more than can be produced by any number of coats of the purest paint. The canvass on which these cloths are produced is manufactured almost exclusively at Dundee; and as it is made eight yards wide, it allows the manufacturer to make his cloths suitable for all probable purposes without the necessity of seaming. One of the finest of this class of productions is unquestionably the one shown by Messrs. Smith and Baber. This cloth is suspended in the carriage riage court at the north-west corner of the Exhibition, and is a remarkable specimen of design, composed principally from forms given by Mr. Lyson, in his admirable work on the Roman villa found in the latter part of the last century near Goodchester. The general arrangement in plan consists of a circular centre formed by guilloches inlaid with tesser, a peculiar vase-like ornament at the corner, a guilloche band, a fine rich outer border of octangular figures, and patter finished by an outer band of well-drawn fret ornament. This design has the merit of being admirably adapted for the purpose of a floor cloth; the colouring, too, exemplifies a fine taste, and as a whole we regard it as an unexceptionably beautiful production. Messrs. Hlare and Co., of Bristol, are the exhi- bitors of some large and varied productions that occupy a prominent position in the gallery north- west of the transept. In these we have every variety of ?? and Roman pavements, carpet patterns, well-drawn parqueterie designs and imitations of inlaid flooring ; also some nicely designed Alhambra scroll ornament. It is evident that no one of these productions is intended to be viewed as a whole in respect to design; and, as an arrangement of patterns, we think that consider- able skill is shown in the combination, whilst many of them are such as will rank among the best of this class of productions. We have looked with considerable interest to the' attempt to manufacture floorcloth with white zinc paint, the result being one of much moment to the artizans engaged in this work, as the material now in use is highly injurious to health, and no doubt l seriously affects the duration of life of the persons so employed. We regret to state, as far as our observations have extended, that the attempts to make floorcloths of spelter paint have failed- first, on account of the appearance the cloth presents, and secondly on account of increased cost in production. A cloth printed with the ma- terial in question has none of the fine glossy surface shown by the cloths made of the ordinary white lead, but looks as if the paint had been mixed with turpentine only, having the appearance of being what painters denominate " flatted"-and that, too when a much greater relative quantity of oil had been used. We have been informed, however, that this cloth presented the appearance of being " seasoned" at the end of four months, quite as much so as the ordinary cloth does at the end of seven or eight. But if even the matter of appear- ance-for we cannot speak as to wear, as yet-did I not militate against the use of zinc paint for floor- cloths, we fear that the increased cost of produc- tion would be fatal; for not only is the zinc paint about 8 per cent. dearer, but it requires a much larger quantity of oil in the working. We state this as being the result of experiments made on a large scale; but we still hope that attention to the manufacture of the paint in question may ulti- mately enable the painter of floorcloths to avail himself of the benefits that arise to health in using it, as compared with the ordinary white lead. STATUAUY PORCELAIN. The large amount of attention which the specimens formed I of this very beautiful material attract in the collection of Mr. Alderman Copeland, .P., Mr. Hinton, and Messrs. Rose and Co., and other exhibitors-as well as the wide i field which it throws open for the cultivation of a love of the fine arts among those to whom the productions of the sculptor are inaccessible-induces us to give sorme additional information with respect to this class of articles. The substance known as statuary porcelain was first in- vented by Mr. Thomas Battam, the manager of Mr. Alderma i Copeland's extensive ceramic manafartory at Stoke-upon- i Trent, and was prominently brought under public notice by the Art Union of London, which gave as one of its prizes a copy of Gibson's Narcissus, formed of this material. The principal ingredients in this composition are kaolin, felspar, and silica, ground and mixed together in the ordi- nary method adopted in the general processes of this manu- facture. It is prepared for the use of the figure makers in a state technically called " slip," about the consistency of I thick cream. In this state it is poured into the different moulds forming the sub-divisions of the figure or group, i which, being made of gypsum (plaster of Paris), rapidly ab- I sorb a portion of the moisture, and reduce the coating im- i mediately next the mould to a semi-clay state, of a suffi. cient thickness for the " cast," when the superfluous " slip" is them poured back from the moulds. This cast remains in the mould for some time at a high temperature, which, by causing still further evaporation, gradually reduces the " slip"I to a state of " clay" sufficiently firm to support its own weight alien relieved from the moulds, and to bear the necessary pressure of the handling without injury. The various parts (and in some groups there are as many as fifty) are then deli- vered from the moulds.
